slides.title: The importance of oil in people's lives
slides.body: Oil is a key element for human life, used to produce fuels for transportation and heating, and to manufacture plastics, industrial products, and even medicines and fertilizers. It has also been the pretext for countless wars and has the power to destabilize the global economy.

slides.title: Open debate about its future
slides.body: It is in this context, and considering the irrefutable reality that it is a non-renewable resource, that the debate arises: When will oil run out, and what will happen when it does, given the enormous dependence on it?

slides.title: Climate change, relentless in its impact on the Himalayas
slides.body: The retreat of the Himalayan glaciers, which are losing mass year after year, is another major threat of climate change, as is the melting of the polar ice caps. Experts warn of the ecological and economic consequences of losing these icy treasures.

image.title: Melting ice in the Himalayan mountain range
image.caption: The effects of climate change are becoming increasingly evident worldwide. One of the effects most frequently emphasized by scientists is the melting of the polar ice caps, but there is another place—no less important for the planet—where glaciers are also melting too rapidly: the Himalayas.

slides.title: Approaching the critical threshold
slides.body: A recent study, reported by the BBC, has warned that the world's highest mountain range is dangerously approaching a critical threshold due to this rapid melting, which could pose a potential danger to people living under its influence.

image.title: The “third pole”
image.caption: The vast Hindu Kush-Himalaya (HKH) region is nicknamed the "third pole" because of its immense snow and ice reserves. But due to climate change, these reserves are melting at an accelerating rate. According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), ice loss there has doubled since 2000.

slides.title: What happened in Nepal is just a warning
slides.body: A prime example of this was the devastating flash flood that killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal after one of the glacial lakes in this mountain range burst. The instability caused there by the melting ice, which ultimately led to the dramatic incident, serves as a warning of what may be to come.

slides.title: Mercedes (1886)
slides.body:
This is where it all started – the first company to build a car. Karl Benz built his first car in 1885 and he patented it in January 1886, but the Mercedes-Benz name wouldn't be adopted until 1901.

That first car (called the Patent Motorwagen, pictured here) had just three wheels and a 0.75 HP 954cc single-cylinder engine, but in 1893 Benz built his first four-wheeler, the Viktoria, powered by a 3 HP 1745cc engine.

slides.title: Peugeot (1891)

Peugeot started out in 1842 making salt and pepper grinders before moving into bicycle production 40 years later. Then in 1891 Peugeot built its first car, a four-wheeled machine with a rear-mounted V-twin engine driving the rear wheels via a chain.

Just five cars were made in that first year, but this grew to 29 in 1892. By 1900 Peugeot production was up to 500 cars in one year.

cards.title: Rules you'd have to follow if you were Amish
cards.abstract: The Amish came to the US from Europe during the 19th century after separating from the Anabaptist church. They set up their own farms and communities, and have lived in very much the same way ever since. Their population has grown rapidly, and there are over 400,000 living in the US today. The Amish stand out due to their strict attire and their rejection of technology. Their relative isolation from the rest of American society has provoked intrigue over the decades, as the contrast between their way of life compared with their neighbors becomes more extreme. Indeed, the rules and traditions of the Amish can seem totally bizarre to an outsider. Click through this gallery to find out what life might be like if you were Amish.
